notes: Passing off between related McAlpine construction companies; shared goodwill, re-branding, and injunctive relief are clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: McAlpine passing off over shared construction name re-branding
key_facts: Sir Robert McAlpine Ltd and Alfred McAlpine Plc are related construction groups that historically distinguished themselves using the forenames Robert and Alfred.
In October 2003 Alfred re-branded publicly as McAlpine without the Alfred identifier, using a new logo and trading style across its business streams.
Robert commenced passing off proceedings seeking an injunction requiring Alfred to use an adequate distinguisher when trading as McAlpine.
Both groups shared goodwill in the McAlpine name and overlapped in construction, civil engineering, PFI, and property development work.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory speedy trial of a passing off claim for final injunctive relief.
enrichment.outcome: Passing off established; injunction granted restraining Alfred from trading as McAlpine without an adequate distinguisher in the relevant commercial fields.
enrichment.ratio: Where two businesses share goodwill in a name, one co-owner may commit passing off by using the shared name without a distinguisher in a market where the name is capable of referring to the other; damage is not limited to direct loss of custom and may include injurious association, reputational risk, and erosion of the co-owner's exclusive value in the goodwill.
legal_issues: Whether Alfred's re-branding as McAlpine without Alfred amounted to a misrepresentation
Whether shared goodwill in the McAlpine name permitted one group to use the name alone
Who constituted the relevant public for passing off in the construction industry
Whether anticipated reputational and exclusivity damage sufficed for quia timet relief

notes: Long-term gas supply contract construction and arbitration jurisdiction under section 32 Arbitration Act 1996 are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Esso gas price review notice and arbitration jurisdiction
key_facts: Esso and the Irish Electricity Supply Board entered a 15-year natural gas supply contract with periodic price review mechanisms.
Esso served a Price Review Notice under clause 12.6 claiming the Energy Charge had fallen to 85% or less of the Comparator.
ESB rejected the notice because Esso calculated the Comparator from short-term spot market prices rather than actual long-term contract prices.
Esso applied under section 32(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996 for a declaration that the tribunal had jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 32(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996 for a declaration as to arbitral jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Esso's Price Review Notice was invalid and the arbitrators lacked jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: Under clause 12.6 of the gas supply contract, a valid Price Review Notice requires the seller to be reasonably satisfied on reasonable grounds that the Energy Charge has diverged to the required extent from the Comparator, which means the actual market price for natural gas currently being supplied under comparable long-term contracts rather than a notional price derived from short-term deliveries.
legal_issues: Whether compliance with clause 12.6(6) was a precondition to a valid Price Review Notice
Meaning of reasonably satisfied in clause 12.6(6)
Whether the Comparator was an actual or notional market price
Whether arbitrators had jurisdiction if the notice was invalid
linked_authorities: The Arpad [1934] P 189
Attorney-General of the Republic of Ghana v Texaco Overseas Tankships Ltd (The Texaco Melbourne) [1994] 1 Lloyd's Rep 473

confidence.notes: The dispute turned on a narrow contractual construction point and the court's conclusions on validity and jurisdiction are explicit.

notes: Contract killing minimum term appeal under section 109 and the Practice Statement tariff guidance are straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Minimum term appeal for contract killing of pregnant victim
key_facts: Michael Stapley was convicted of conspiracy to murder Soumia Cullinane, who was 34 weeks pregnant, in a contract killing arranged by her husband.
Stapley received a mandatory life sentence with a 15-year minimum term under section 109 because of a prior serious offence conviction.
The killing involved brutal multiple injuries, body disposal, and payment of £10,000 to co-accused killers.
Stapley appealed on the sole ground that the 15-year minimum term was too long.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave against minimum term on a mandatory life sentence for conspiracy to murder.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the 15-year minimum term was not manifestly excessive.
enrichment.ratio: In sentencing for conspiracy to murder where the murder is carried out, the court should have regard to murder tariff guidance in the Practice Statement; a contract killing of a vulnerable heavily pregnant victim with extensive injuries and recent serious offending justified a very substantial minimum term, with only limited mitigation for youth.
legal_issues: Whether conspiracy to murder should be sentenced by reference to murder tariff starting points
Application of section 109 mandatory life sentence provisions
Appropriate minimum term for a contract killing with aggravating features
Effect of prior serious offence conviction on automatic life sentence

notes: Legally aided brief fee assessment in the oral contraceptive group litigation; Loveday principles applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Lord Brennan QC brief fee in contraceptive pill litigation
key_facts: Lord Brennan QC acted as leading counsel for 135 legally aided claimants in group litigation over third-generation oral contraceptive pills.
After a 42-day trial MacKay J dismissed the claims on epidemiological and biological plausibility grounds.
The costs judge reduced Brennan's claimed £250,000 brief fee to £199,500 and disallowed separate fees for expert conferences and a case management conference.
Brennan appealed the assessment of post-brief fees under regulation 107 of the Civil Legal Aid General Regulations 1989.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a legal aid detailed costs assessment by a costs judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the brief fee of £250,000 less £500 was restored, but separate fees for expert conferences and the CMC were not allowed.
enrichment.ratio: On legal aid taxation, meetings with experts and case management conferences after delivery of the brief are ordinarily part of trial preparation covered by the brief fee under Loveday v Renton (No 2); brief fees should be assessed by reference to the full history of the trial and CPR 44.5 factors, not by converting preparation time into an hourly rate that deducts counsel's pre-eminence.
legal_issues: Whether expert conference fees after brief delivery were recoverable separately
Whether a case management conference fee was recoverable separately from the brief fee
Correct approach to assessing a leading counsel's brief fee on the standard basis
Whether hourly rate analysis was appropriate for brief fee assessment

notes: Immigration appeal leave rules where representation changed mid-process; Ravichandran and Rule 18(6) analysis is detailed but outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: IAT leave to appeal after change of representative
key_facts: A Somali asylum seeker dismissed by an adjudicator sought leave to appeal to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal.
Former solicitors lodged grounds just within time, then the Law Centre submitted separate grounds after the appellant changed representation.
The Vice-President refused leave having considered only the first solicitor's grounds, despite the Tribunal later accepting the Law Centre as representative.
Mackay J dismissed judicial review, but the Court of Appeal held the Tribunal should have put both sets of grounds before the decision-maker.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from dismissal of judicial review of Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to the Tribunal for fresh consideration of leave to appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 18(6) of the Immigration and Asylum Appeals (Procedure) Rules 2002 is not an exclusionary rule; once the Tribunal accepted the new representative who had submitted timely grounds, the Vice-President should have been provided with those grounds to decide whether to exercise discretion to consider them, notwithstanding an earlier apparently valid application by the former representative.
legal_issues: Effect of Rule 35(4) and (6) when an appellant changes representative
Whether Rule 18(6) prevented consideration of later grounds of appeal
Whether failure to put Law Centre grounds before the Vice-President was an administrative or procedural error under Rule 19
Application of Ravichandran principles to procedural non-compliance

notes: Capital allowances plant versus premises test for all-weather racecourse; tax authorities and outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Capital allowances for all-weather horse racing track
key_facts: Lingfield Park (1991) Ltd claimed capital allowances on about £2.96m spent installing an all-weather race track at Lingfield Park Racecourse.
General Commissioners held the all-weather track was plant under section 24 of the Capital Allowances Act 1990.
Hart J reversed the decision on appeal, holding the track functioned as premises rather than apparatus.
The dispute concerned whether the artificial equitrack surface, drainage, and fencing were plant or part of the racecourse premises.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from High Court decision on a case stated by General Commissioners.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the all-weather track was not plant and the capital allowances claim failed.
enrichment.ratio: Applying the premises test in capital allowances cases, an all-weather horse racing track installed on a racecourse functions as premises on which the trade is carried on rather than as apparatus with which the trade is carried on, even though it is artificial, separately constructed, and not land in its natural state.
legal_issues: Whether the all-weather track satisfied the business use test
Whether the track functioned as plant or premises under the premises test
Whether General Commissioners' plant finding was a matter of fact and degree immune from interference
Relevance of comparables such as swimming pools, dry docks, and car wash sites

notes: Section 29 NHS professional regulation appeal on unduly lenient nurse misconduct sanction; borderline but clear dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: CRHP appeal over lenient nurse pornography misconduct sanction

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service Reform and Health Care Professions Act 2002
Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors (Professional Conduct) Rules 1993 Approval Order 1993

key_facts: Mr Truscott, a paediatric nurse, admitted using a hospital computer on an adolescent ward to access pornographic websites over several nights in March 2002.
The Nursing and Midwifery Council Professional Conduct Committee found misconduct proved and imposed a five-year caution rather than removal from the register.
The Council for the Regulation of Healthcare Professionals appealed under section 29 alleging the penalty was unduly lenient.
CRHP argued the accessed material raised child protection concerns and showed poor judgment by a nurse working with vulnerable adolescents.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 29 of the NHS Reform and Health Care Professions Act 2002 against a professional conduct committee penalty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; undue leniency was not established despite the case being borderline and properly referred.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 29 appeal the court applies an unduly lenient test analogous to criminal appeals in aggravation; a caution may be lenient without being unduly so where the committee could reasonably regard adult pornography accessed on duty as serious misconduct warranting caution but not mandatory removal, especially where deliberate access to child pornography was not established on the evidence before the committee.
legal_issues: Scope of section 29 powers to refer unduly lenient professional disciplinary decisions
Whether the unduly lenient test applied rather than ordinary CPR appellate review
Whether a caution was unduly lenient for accessing pornography on a paediatric ward
Extent to which aggravating material not fully addressed by the committee could be relied on

notes: Parole Board re-release challenge under section 44A CJA 1991 and Article 5; Sim principles applied comprehensively.

enrichment.short_title: Parole Board re-release challenge after licence revocation
key_facts: Alan Jarvis was detained for rape and indecent assault on young boys and released on licence after serving half of a three-and-a-half-year custodial term.
His licence was revoked after he was arrested for allegedly indecently assaulting an 11-year-old boy; the CPS later discontinued prosecution.
The Parole Board refused re-release, finding he presented a high risk of sexual re-offending that could not safely be managed in the community.
Jarvis challenged the decision as unlawful and in breach of Article 5, arguing the Board used the wrong comparative risk approach.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Parole Board refusal to direct re-release under section 44A of the Criminal Justice Act 1991.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the Parole Board lawfully applied section 44A(4) and there was no Article 5 breach.
enrichment.ratio: On re-release of a recalled extended-sentence prisoner, the Parole Board must apply section 44A(4) and ask whether confinement remains necessary for public protection based on all current evidence; there is no requirement to compare current risk with that at sentencing, and recall for breach of licence or fresh risk concerns does not break the causal link with the original sentence for Article 5 purposes.
legal_issues: Correct approach under section 44A(4) to re-release after licence revocation
Whether the Board had to compare risk at sentencing with risk at review
Effect of discontinued prosecution on recall and re-release decision
Whether Article 5 required a presumption in favour of release where the Board was uncertain

notes: Compulsory purchase compensation timing issue; split reasoning on post-valuation planning evidence but appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Compulsory purchase compensation and post-valuation planning evidence
key_facts: Swansea City compulsorily purchased two parcels of grazing land at Llansamlet for a Tawe Vale development scheme.
The Lands Tribunal valued the larger parcel at £500,000 assuming residential development could be implemented within about two years.
The acquiring authority appealed, arguing the member wrongly relied on 1998 planning permission for Tregof Farm granted after the February 1996 valuation date.
The dispute concerned whether piecemeal residential development would have been permitted quickly in a no-scheme world.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Lands Tribunal determination of compulsory purchase compensation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; compensation based on a two-year implementation assumption was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: When assessing open market value at the valuation date, post-valuation planning events cannot directly inform what a hypothetical purchaser would have anticipated; however, where a tribunal's primary planning judgment rests on contemporaneous plans, housing need, and site suitability, an error in using later permission as confirmatory evidence will not disturb the outcome if the same conclusion would inevitably have been reached without it.
legal_issues: Whether the member took into account impermissible post-valuation planning permission
Application of Pointe Gourde principles to planning judgment versus valuation
When residential development of countryside land would have been permitted
Whether piecemeal development concerns justified a ten-year delay

notes: Youth defendant special measures and video link availability; statutory exclusion and Article 6 analysis are thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Youth defendant denied special measures video link

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: A 13-year-old girl with learning difficulties was charged with two robberies alongside three older co-defendants in youth court proceedings.
She said she wished to give evidence against co-defendants but was too scared to do so in their presence and would otherwise not testify.
The district judge granted special measures for complainants but held the 1999 Act gave no power to grant a defendant a video-link direction.
She sought judicial review of the refusal and of the judge's further refusal to order evidence by live link at common law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of youth court refusal to permit defendant to give evidence by video link under statutory special measures or common law.
enrichment.outcome: Relief refused; defendants are excluded from the special measures regime and no common law power exists to direct defendant evidence by live link.
enrichment.ratio: The Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999 deliberately excludes accused persons from special measures, and Parliament's subsequent statutory regulation of live-link evidence in criminal trials is incompatible with a parallel common law power; fairness under Article 6 must be judged retrospectively after trial, and section 3 cannot be used to read defendants into the special measures scheme.
legal_issues: Whether a defendant co-accused could receive a special measures direction under the 1999 Act
Whether the court had inherent power to permit defendant evidence by live link
Whether exclusion of defendants from special measures breached Article 6 or equality of arms
Whether section 3 Human Rights Act permitted a conforming interpretation of section 16
